standard_text: Compare and order rational numbers and plot them on a number line. Write, interpret, and explain statements of order for rational numbers in real-world contexts.

progression.narrative: This standard asks students to plot rational numbers on a number line, compare and order them, and write and explain statements of order in real contexts like temperature, elevation, and money. The on-grade work runs from plotting and two-number comparison up through ordering mixed lists and writing inequalities from situations, with the central bug being digit comparison on negatives, such as calling -8 greater than -3. Students who struggle here usually carry gaps from well below grade six: shaky whole-number place value and no picture of a fraction as a position on a line. Intervention should rebuild those foundations, then the grade five skills of comparing decimals by place value and ordering positive fractions and decimals together, and only then reintroduce the negative side of the line.

steps.rationale: The standard says 'plot them on a number line' -- and position is what every later comparison leans on. A student who can't place -6 left of -3 has no ground to stand on when comparing them.
The core act of the standard: compare two rational numbers and capture the result with < or >. This is where the 'bigger digits means bigger number' bug must be confronted head-on with negatives.
The standard says students must 'interpret' statements of order. Judging someone else's comparison as true or false, across a table of several values, is interpretation in its most testable form.

The standard says 'order rational numbers' -- more than two at a time, mixing fractions, decimals, and negatives. Ordering forces students to put every number into one comparable form and respect the flip on the negative side.

The standard's real-world demand: WRITE statements of order from contexts -- elevations, bank balances, temperatures -- and from positional language like 'to the left of.' Producing the inequality is a step beyond recognizing it.
The standard says 'explain statements of order.' Defending which of two close numbers (like -72 and -71.99) is greater, using distance from zero, is the DOK 3 top of this standard.

skills.name: Compare multi-digit whole numbers using place value

prerequisite_skill.description: Compare two whole numbers up to four digits using place value and record the result with < or >.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: Which is greater, 350 or 530? How do you know?

skills.i_do_script: To compare whole numbers, I compare places, starting from the biggest place. Watch: for 350 and 530, both have three digits, so I compare the hundreds first. 3 hundreds against 5 hundreds: 5 hundreds is more, so 530 is greater, and I write 350 < 530. If the biggest places tie, I move one place to the right and compare again. The symbol always opens toward the greater number, and I read it left to right as a sentence: 350 is less than 530.

canonical_error.pattern: Compares stray digits instead of matching places, or points the symbol the wrong way
canonical_error.example: Writes 105 < 89 because 8 and 9 look bigger than 1 and 0
canonical_error.why: The student scans for big digits instead of lining up places. A digit in the hundreds place outweighs any digit in the tens place, so 105 has more just by having a hundred.

skills.item_template: Two whole numbers up to four digits with a blank between them. Student writes < or >, or picks the greater number. Short response fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: Write < or >: 105 __ 89
Write < or >: 72 __ 27
Which is greater: 2301 or 2031?
Order from least to greatest: 340, 304, 430
Write < or >: 68 __ 71

redirect_script.stop: Which place did you compare first?
redirect_script.prompt: Line the numbers up by place value and compare the biggest place first. If it ties, slide one place to the right. Then read your symbol out loud as a sentence and check that the sentence is true.
redirect_script.praise: You compared the biggest place first and the symbol told the truth.

vocabulary.definition: The amount a digit is worth because of its position: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands.
The symbol that says the first number is bigger. 530 > 350 reads 530 is greater than 350.
The symbol that says the first number is smaller. 350 < 530 reads 350 is less than 530.

next_steps.if_fail: Review grade 4 place value with base ten blocks: build both numbers, then compare hundreds to hundreds and tens to tens.

worked_example_script.text: Write 350 and 530 in a place value chart, hundreds tens ones, one number above the other.
Which place do we compare first, and why not the ones?
The hundreds place carries the most value. 3 hundreds against 5 hundreds: 530 wins before we even look at the tens. So 350 < 530.
If a student picks 350 because the 5 in the tens catches their eye, point at the chart: a 5 in the tens is 50, a 5 in the hundreds is 500.
Your turn: use the chart to compare 468 and 486, then write the symbol and read the sentence out loud.

skills.name: Represent fractions as positions on a number line

prerequisite_skill.description: Place fractions like 1/2, 1/4, and 3/4 on a number line from 0 to 1 by cutting the line into equal parts.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: On a number line from 0 to 1, where does 3/4 go?

skills.i_do_script: A fraction is a spot on the number line, not just a piece of pizza. Watch me place 3/4 on a line from 0 to 1: the denominator says cut the space from 0 to 1 into 4 equal parts, and the numerator says hop 3 of those parts from 0. I count the hops out loud: 1/4, 2/4, 3/4. My mark lands three hops past 0, most of the way to 1. Count spaces, not tick marks, and always start the hops at 0.

canonical_error.pattern: Counts tick marks instead of spaces, or thinks a bigger denominator means a bigger fraction
canonical_error.example: Places 1/4 to the right of 1/2 because 4 is more than 2
canonical_error.why: The student reads the denominator as a size instead of a number of cuts. More cuts make smaller pieces, so 1/4 is a shorter hop from 0 than 1/2. The line settles it: 1/4 lands left of 1/2.

skills.item_template: A number line from 0 to 1 (or 0 to 2) cut into halves, thirds, fourths, sixths, or eighths. Student names a marked point or places a given fraction. Positive fractions only.

sample_items.stem: A number line from 0 to 1 is cut into 4 equal parts. What fraction is 1 hop from 0?
On a number line from 0 to 1, where does 1/2 go?
A number line from 0 to 1 is cut into 4 equal parts. What fraction is 3 hops from 0?
On a number line from 0 to 1, is 3/4 closer to 0 or closer to 1?
Which is farther right on the number line: 1/2 or 1/4?
A number line from 0 to 1 is cut into 3 equal parts. What fraction is 2 hops from 0?
On a number line from 0 to 2, where does 3/2 go?
A number line from 0 to 1 is cut into 8 equal parts. What fraction is 4 hops from 0? What simpler fraction lands at the same spot?

redirect_script.stop: How many equal parts is the line cut into, and where do your hops start?
redirect_script.prompt: The bottom number tells how many equal parts to cut the space from 0 to 1 into. The top number tells how many hops from 0. Count the spaces, not the marks, and hop out loud from 0.
redirect_script.praise: You cut the line into equal parts and counted hops from 0, that is exactly what a fraction means.

vocabulary.definition: The bottom number of a fraction. It tells how many equal parts the space from 0 to 1 is cut into.
The top number of a fraction. It counts how many parts, or hops from 0, you take.
The space between two tick marks. Count spaces, not marks, to find a value.

next_steps.if_fail: Fold a paper strip into halves and fourths, label each fold, and lay the strip along a drawn number line before returning to these items.

worked_example_script.text: Draw a number line from 0 to 1. Cut the space into 4 equal parts with tick marks.
How many equal spaces did we make? Count the spaces with me, not the marks.
Four equal spaces, so each hop is worth 1/4. To place 3/4, I start at 0 and hop three times: 1/4, 2/4, 3/4. The mark lands three quarters of the way to 1.
If a student counts tick marks and lands wrong, have them hop a finger space by space, saying each fraction out loud from 0.
Your turn: on this same line, place 1/2. Is it left or right of 3/4?

skills.name: Compare positive decimals to the thousandths using place value

prerequisite_skill.description: Compare two positive decimals to the thousandths by comparing place values, and record the result with < or >.

skills.i_do_script: Decimals compare place by place, just like whole numbers, starting from the biggest place. Watch me compare 0.5 and 0.35: I compare the tenths first. 5 tenths against 3 tenths: 5 tenths is more, so 0.5 is greater, even though 35 looks bigger than 5. On a hundredths grid, 0.5 shades 50 squares and 0.35 shades only 35. If the tenths tie, I slide right to the hundredths, then the thousandths. More digits never means a bigger decimal.

canonical_error.pattern: Compares decimals like whole numbers, deciding the one with more digits or bigger looking digits is greater
canonical_error.why: Whole number habits: for every number the student met early on, more digits meant more. Decimals break that rule because places to the right are smaller. Tenths outweigh hundredths no matter how many digits follow.

skills.item_template: Two positive decimals to the thousandths, often with the digit-count trap (0.4 vs 0.35) or tied leading places (2.5 vs 2.48). Student writes < or > or picks the greater decimal. NR or MC.

sample_items.stem: Which decimal is greatest?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 0.099 baits the most-digits rule; 0.445 baits students who read 445 as bigger than 5; 0.35 baits 35 > 5

sample_items.stem: Order from least to greatest: 0.4, 0.04, 0.44
Which comparison is TRUE?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 0.702 > 0.72 baits the more-digits rule; 0.072 > 0.72 tests whether a leading zero place is understood; = baits students who see the same digits

redirect_script.stop: Which place are you comparing first?
redirect_script.prompt: Line up the decimal points and compare place by place from the left: tenths first, then hundredths, then thousandths. Append zeros if you need them, 0.5 is the same as 0.50. Then decide.
redirect_script.praise: You compared tenths to tenths instead of counting digits, that is the whole skill.

vocabulary.definition: The first place to the right of the decimal point. One tenth is 1/10 or 0.1.
The second place to the right of the decimal point. One hundredth is 1/100 or 0.01.
The third place to the right of the decimal point. One thousandth is 1/1000 or 0.001.

worked_example_script.text: Shade 0.5 on one hundredths grid and 0.35 on another, side by side.
Which grid has more shading? So which number is greater?
0.5 shades 50 of the 100 squares and 0.35 shades 35. The tenths digit decides it: 5 tenths beats 3 tenths, so 0.5 > 0.35.
If a student says 0.35 is greater because 35 > 5, send them back to the grids: which one covers more?
Your turn: which is greater, 0.6 or 0.58? Prove it with places, then with a grid if you need it.

practice_problems.stem: Order from least to greatest: 2.3, 2.03, 2.33
Write a decimal between 0.6 and 0.61.
practice_problems.answer: Any decimal between them, such as 0.605

practice_problems.stem: Mia wrote 0.35 > 0.5. Find her mistake and fix it.
shown_work: Mia said: 35 is bigger than 5, so 0.35 is bigger.
practice_problems.answer: Mia compared the digits like whole numbers. Compare the tenths place first: 3 tenths against 5 tenths, so 0.35 < 0.5. On a hundredths grid, 0.5 covers 50 squares and 0.35 covers only 35.

activities.title: Grid Duel
activities.instructions:
1. Each partner draws a decimal card, like 0.5 or 0.35.
2. Both shade their decimal on a hundredths grid.
3. Lay the grids side by side: the grid with more shading holds the greater decimal.
4. Write the true comparison, like 0.35 < 0.5, and read it out loud.
5. After five rounds, try a round with no grids, places only, then check one with a grid.

activities.title: Trap or True
materials: 12 comparison cards, half true and half written by the more-digits rule
activities.instructions:
1. Spread the TRUE and FALSE headers.
2. Take turns drawing a card like 0.099 > 0.1, reading it as a sentence, and sorting it.
3. A challenge means both students compare place by place before the card lands.
4. Debrief: every FALSE card was written by the same wrong rule. Name the rule and say why it fails for decimals.

strategy_links.why: Hundredths grids make 'tenths outweigh hundredths' visible before the compare-by-place rule is named.
The more-digits-means-bigger error is stable and predictable; finding and fixing it head-on breaks the whole number habit.
Quick whiteboard rounds of two-decimal comparisons show instantly who is still counting digits.

questioning_prompts: Which place are you comparing first, and why that one?
Why can you write 0.5 as 0.50 without changing its value?
Which covers more of the grid, 0.5 or 0.35? What does that tell you?
The tenths tied. Where do you look next?
Can a decimal with three digits be smaller than a decimal with one digit? Show me an example.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student says the decimal with more digits is greater, like 0.35 > 0.5.
misconception_redirects.say: Shade both on hundredths grids. Which covers more squares? Now compare the tenths place: 5 tenths beats 3 tenths.
misconception_redirects.praise: You let the places decide instead of the digit count.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student compares correctly but points the symbol the wrong way.
misconception_redirects.say: Read your statement out loud, left to right. Does the sentence tell the truth? Flip the symbol until it does.
misconception_redirects.praise: You made the symbol say exactly what you meant.

quick_checks.look_for: 0.4 > 0.35 by comparing tenths. The answer < means the more-digits rule is still running.
0.61, found by comparing hundredths after the tenths tie, not by comparing 61 to 607.

worked_solution.stem: Which is greater, 0.5 or 0.35? Write the true comparison.

steps.annotation: Append a zero so both decimals show hundredths. 0.5 and 0.50 are the same value.
Start at the biggest place. 5 tenths is more, so the comparison is already decided.
On a hundredths grid, 0.5 shades 50 squares and 0.35 shades 35.
The sentence tells the truth, so the symbol faces the right way.

faded_example.stem: Which is greater, 0.6 or 0.58? Write the true comparison.

steps.annotation: Append a zero so both decimals show hundredths.
Start at the biggest place.
Which is greater? Write the comparison with the symbol.
Read your statement out loud to check it.

sentence_starters: I compared the ___ place first, and ___ tenths is more than ___ tenths.
More digits does not mean greater, because ___.

skills.name: Order positive fractions and decimals on a number line

prerequisite_skill.description: Place positive fractions and decimals on the same number line and order them, using renaming and the benchmarks 0, 1/2, and 1.

skills.i_do_script: To order fractions and decimals together, I put them in one costume first. Watch me order 3/4, 0.5, and 0.7: I rename 3/4 as 0.75, because 3/4 of 100 is 75. Now all three are decimals: 0.5, 0.7, 0.75. On a number line from 0 to 1, 0.5 sits halfway, 0.7 is two hops past it, and 0.75 is just past 0.7. Least to greatest: 0.5, 0.7, 3/4. Rename first, place second, and let the positions do the ordering.

canonical_error.pattern: Orders fractions by their digits, or refuses to put fractions and decimals on the same line
canonical_error.example: Says 0.7 > 3/4 because 7 is bigger than 3, or orders 1/2 before 1/4 because 2 is less than 4
canonical_error.why: The student treats fractions and decimals as different kinds of objects with no shared home. Both are positions on the same line: 3/4 = 0.75 sits to the right of 0.7, so 3/4 is greater. Renaming into one form makes every comparison a position check.

skills.item_template: Three or four positive numbers mixing fractions and decimals (halves, fourths, fifths, tenths, decimals to hundredths). Student orders them, places them on a marked number line, or picks the correct ordered list. MC or NR.

sample_items.stem: Which is greater: 3/4 or 0.7?
Write 1/2 as a decimal.
Order from least to greatest: 0.5, 1/4, 0.8
Which list shows the numbers in order from least to greatest?
sample_items.distractor_logic: The second list orders fractions before decimals as separate kinds; the third baits students who place 1/2 by its digits after 0.6; the fourth is greatest to least

sample_items.stem: Is 2/5 more or less than 1/2?
On a number line from 0 to 1, which is farther right: 0.65 or 3/5?
Order from greatest to least: 0.9, 4/5, 0.85
Which number is between 1/2 and 3/4 on the number line?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 0.4 and 1/4 sit left of 1/2; 0.8 sits right of 3/4; each catches a student who cannot place the benchmarks

redirect_script.stop: Are all your numbers in the same form yet?
redirect_script.prompt: Rename every fraction as a decimal, or every decimal as a fraction, so they all wear one costume. Then place them on the line from 0 to 1 and read the order left to right.
redirect_script.praise: You renamed first and let the positions do the ordering, that is the whole move.

vocabulary.definition: Naming the same value in a different form. 3/4, 0.75, and 75/100 all sit at the same point on the line.
A friendly anchor value like 0, 1/2, or 1 that you compare other numbers against.
Arrange numbers from least to greatest or greatest to least. On a horizontal line, least to greatest reads left to right.

worked_example_script.text: Draw a number line from 0 to 1 with ticks every tenth. Write the list to order: 3/4, 0.5, 0.7.
Can we place 3/4 on this tenths line as it is? What could we rename it as?
3/4 is 75 out of 100, so 3/4 = 0.75. Now place all three: 0.5 at the halfway tick, 0.7 two ticks past it, and 0.75 halfway between 0.7 and 0.8. Reading left to right: 0.5, 0.7, 3/4.
If a student says 0.7 beats 3/4 because 7 beats 3, point at the line: which mark is farther right?
Your turn: rename 2/5 as a decimal and place it. Is it left or right of 0.5?

practice_problems.stem: Write 3/4 as a decimal.
Which is greater: 1/2 or 0.4?
Order from least to greatest: 0.7, 3/4, 0.6
Order from least to greatest: 1/4, 0.3, 1/5
On a number line from 0 to 1, place 0.45 and 1/2. Which is farther right?
practice_problems.answer: 1/2, because 1/2 = 0.5 and 0.5 is right of 0.45

practice_problems.stem: Order from greatest to least: 4/5, 0.75, 0.9
Write a number between 3/5 and 0.7.
practice_problems.answer: Any number between 0.6 and 0.7, such as 0.65

practice_problems.stem: Leo ordered 0.7, 3/4, 0.5 from least to greatest and wrote: 3/4, 0.5, 0.7. Find his mistake and fix it.
shown_work: Leo said: 3 is the smallest number I see, so 3/4 goes first.
practice_problems.answer: Leo compared the digit 3 instead of the value of 3/4. Rename: 3/4 = 0.75, which is the greatest of the three. Correct order: 0.5, 0.7, 3/4.

activities.title: One Line, Two Costumes
materials: Clothesline or taped line labeled 0, 1/2, and 1
activities.instructions:
1. Hang the 0, 1/2, and 1 anchors on the line.
2. Partners take turns drawing a card and pinning it where it belongs, saying the renaming out loud, like 3/4 is 0.75, so it goes past 0.7.
3. The partner may challenge; a challenge means both rename and check against the benchmarks.
4. When all cards hang, read the whole line left to right as a least to greatest list.
5. Debrief: which card was hardest to place, and what renaming settled it?

activities.title: Costume Match
materials: Card deck: fraction cards and decimal cards, plus two decoys
activities.instructions:
1. Spread all cards face up.
2. Match each fraction to the decimal that sits at the same point on the line, saying how you know, like 1/4 is 25 out of 100.
3. Two decoy decimals match nothing; set them aside and name the fraction they would match.
4. Debrief: pick any matched pair and show both names landing on one point of a number line.

strategy_links.why: A physical clothesline, then a drawn line, then bare renaming: CRA builds the idea that fractions and decimals share one home.
Short number talks like 'which is greater, 3/4 or 0.7, and how do you SEE it' surface digit-based reasoning where it can be fixed.
Leo's digit-comparison error is exactly the bug that resurfaces with negatives in grade six, so fixing it here pays twice.

questioning_prompts: What costume will you put all these numbers in, fractions or decimals?
Is this number more or less than 1/2? How do you know?
What is 3/4 as a decimal, and how does 75 out of 100 show it?
Which mark is farther right on the line? So which number is greater?
Could you have compared these without renaming, using a benchmark instead?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student compares a fraction and a decimal by their digits, like 0.7 > 3/4 because 7 > 3.
misconception_redirects.say: Rename 3/4 as a decimal first: 75 out of 100 is 0.75. Now place both on the line. Which is farther right?
misconception_redirects.praise: You renamed before you compared, so the positions could tell the truth.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student orders fractions by denominator size, putting 1/4 after 1/2 because 4 > 2.
misconception_redirects.say: More cuts make smaller pieces. Fold a strip in half, then in fourths: which fold is closer to 0? Place both on the line and check.
misconception_redirects.praise: You used the positions, not the denominators, to set the order.

quick_checks.look_for: 3/4, with the renaming 3/4 = 0.75 stated. The answer 0.7 means digits are still driving.
0.45, 1/2, 0.6, with 1/2 renamed as 0.5 and placed between the decimals.

worked_solution.stem: Order 3/4, 0.5, and 0.7 from least to greatest.

steps.annotation: Rename the fraction so every number wears the decimal costume. 3/4 of 100 is 75.

steps.math: Place on the line: 0.5, then 0.7, then 0.75
steps.annotation: 0.5 is halfway to 1, 0.7 is two tenths past it, 0.75 is just past 0.7.
On a horizontal line, least to greatest always reads left to right.
Give the answer in the original names. Renaming was for placing, not for the final list.

faded_example.stem: Order 2/5, 0.35, and 0.5 from least to greatest.

steps.annotation: Rename the fraction as a decimal: 2/5 of 100 is 40.

steps.math: Place on the line: 0.35, then 0.4, then 0.5
steps.annotation: All three now sit on one tenths line.
Read the order left to right.
Write the final list using the original names.

sentence_starters: I renamed ___ as ___ so all the numbers wore one costume.
___ is greater because it sits farther right on the number line.
Compared to the benchmark 1/2, this number is ___.

skills.name: Plot and identify rational numbers on a number line
skills.i_do_script: We're putting numbers -- including negatives -- in their true spots on a number line. Watch me plot -6 and -3: zero is home base, positives count up to the right, negatives count away to the LEFT. From 0 I step left three times to reach -3, and left six times to reach -6. Notice -6 lands FARTHER LEFT than -3, even though 6 is a bigger count than 3. On the negative side, a bigger count means farther from zero, which means farther left.

canonical_error.pattern: Places negatives by count order left to right -- puts -6 to the RIGHT of -3 because 6 comes after 3
canonical_error.example: Asked to plot -3 and -6, the student marks -3 first and then -6 one step to its right, keeping the 'counting up goes right' habit
canonical_error.why: Years of counting up left to right. The student treats the negative side as a copy of the positive side instead of a mirror image -- they don't yet see that on the left of zero, a bigger count means farther LEFT, not farther right.

redirect_script.stop: Stop -- where is zero, and which way did you walk?
redirect_script.prompt: Put your finger on 0. To plot -6, you walk LEFT 6 steps -- count them out loud. Now plot -3 the same way. Which number ended up farther left? The negative side is a mirror: bigger count, farther left.
redirect_script.praise: You counted from zero in the right direction -- that's exactly how the negative side works.

skills.item_template: A number line with integer ticks. Either a labeled point to identify (NR), or a set of integers (positive and negative) to plot/order left to right (MC or plot).

sample_items.stem: The numbers -6, -3, 4, 7 are plotted on the number line below. Which list shows these numbers in order from left to right on the number line?
sample_items.distractor_logic: '-3, -6, 4, 7' is the magnitude-order bait (3 before 6); '7, 4, -3, -6' is fully reversed; '4, 7, -3, -6' puts positives first as if negatives don't count

sample_items.stem: Point P is marked on the number line below. What integer is Point P located at?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Students who ignore the negative side answer 4; miscounting from the left end gives -5 or -3

sample_items.stem: Mark -7 on the number line below.
sample_items.answer: The point one tick to the right of -8 (7 steps left of 0)
sample_items.distractor_logic: Students may count 7 ticks from the left END of the line instead of 7 steps left from 0

sample_items.stem: Which number is farther to the left on a number line: -9 or -2?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Magnitude bait: 9 > 2 tempts students to say -9 is farther RIGHT

sample_items.stem: Point K is marked on the number line below. What number is Point K located at?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Rational ticks every 0.5 -- counting whole ticks gives -2 or -1; ignoring the sign gives 1.5

vocabulary.definition: The whole numbers and their opposites: ..., -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, ...
Mark a number's exact spot on the number line.
On a horizontal number line, farther left always means a smaller value.
On a horizontal number line, farther right always means a greater value.

next_steps.if_pass: Move to 6NS3-S2: turn positions into comparison statements with < and >.
next_steps.if_fail: Check 6NS3-F2 -- if the student can't read positive rational ticks, fix that first. If positives are fine, drill 'start at 0, walk left' with a floor number line before returning.

worked_example_script.text: Draw a number line from -8 to 8 on the board, with 0 circled. Say nothing else yet.
We need to plot -3 and -6. Before we plot anything: where do we always start, and why?
The negative sign in -3 is a direction sign. Which way does it send us from 0?
Walk a finger left from 0, counting out loud: 1, 2, 3. Mark -3.
Now you plot -6 the same way. Count your steps out loud as you go.
If the student marks -6 to the RIGHT of -3, they're counting up left to right. Don't correct -- ask: 'Is -6 six steps from zero? Count again from 0.'
Look at both marks. Which number is farther from zero? And which is farther LEFT? Is that the same answer or different?
On the negative side, farther from zero means farther left. The negative side is a mirror of the positive side -- that's the one idea today.

practice_problems.stem: Point A is marked on the number line below. What integer is Point A located at?
On a number line, is -2 to the left or to the right of 0?
practice_problems.answer: To the left

practice_problems.stem: Point Q is marked on the number line below. What integer is Point Q located at?
practice_problems.notes: Watch for the answer 5 -- the student read distance but dropped the sign.

practice_problems.stem: Mark -6 on the number line below.
practice_problems.answer: The point 6 steps left of 0

practice_problems.stem: The numbers -7, -2, 1, 5 are plotted on a number line. List them in order from left to right.
practice_problems.notes: The bait order is -2, -7, 1, 5 -- negatives sorted by count instead of position.

practice_problems.stem: Devon plotted -5 and -2 on a number line. Find his mistake and fix it.
shown_work: Task: plot -5 and -2 on a number line.
Devon marked -2, then marked -5 to the RIGHT of -2.
Devon said: '5 comes after 2 when I count, so -5 goes farther right.'
practice_problems.answer: -5 belongs to the LEFT of -2. From 0, -5 is five steps left and -2 is only two steps left. On the negative side, a bigger count means farther from zero -- which is farther LEFT, not right.
practice_problems.notes: The canonical error: counting order applied to the negative side.

practice_problems.stem: Point M is marked on the number line below. What number is Point M located at?
practice_problems.notes: Rational ticks -- the spaces are worth 0.5, not 1.

practice_problems.stem: Point X is the same distance from 0 as 4, but on the left side of 0. What number is X?
practice_problems.notes: Builds the opposites idea -- distance equal, direction flipped.

activities.title: Walk the Line
materials: Painter's tape number line on the floor from -10 to 10
activities.instructions:
1. Lay the tape line with 0 marked boldly and ticks every foot.
2. Each student draws a card (like -6) and must START at 0, announce 'left' or 'right,' and walk that many steps out loud.
3. The group checks: did they start at zero? Did they walk the right direction?
4. Twist round: two students walk their cards at once (-3 and -6) and the group says who is farther left and why.
5. Debrief: on the negative side, what does a bigger count do to your position?

activities.title: Where Did Devon Go Wrong?
materials: Printed problem slip with Devon's number line
activities.instructions:
1. Pairs study Devon's plot of -5 and -2 and find the exact moment his thinking broke.
2. Note that his reasoning is sensible on the positive side -- 5 IS to the right of 2. Ask: what changes on the other side of 0?
3. Pairs redraw the line correctly, counting steps from 0 out loud.
4. Debrief question: why does the negative side work like a mirror?

content.worked_problem: Plot -5 and -2 on a number line. Devon marked -5 to the right of -2, saying '5 comes after 2 when I count.'
content.error_step: Devon kept the 'counting up goes right' rule on the negative side of zero.
content.why: Negatives count AWAY from zero to the left. -5 is five steps left of 0, so it lands farther left than -2. The negative side mirrors the positive side.

activities.title: Point-to-Value Match
materials: Cards showing number lines with one labeled point each
activities.instructions:
1. Spread six number-line cards (points at -6, -2.5, -1, 0.5, 3, -0.5) and eight value cards -- two are decoys.
2. Partners match each pictured point to its value, saying HOW they counted ('two and a half steps left of zero').
3. The decoys (6 and 2.5) catch anyone dropping the negative sign.
4. Debrief: which two cards were hardest to tell apart, and what decided it?

strategy_links.why: A concrete floor line, then a drawn line, then bare numbers -- CRA is the natural ramp for position sense with negatives.
Devon's mirror-image error (plotting -5 right of -2) is a perfect find-and-fix target.
Whiteboard rounds of 'sketch a line and plot these two numbers' instantly show who flips the negative side.

questioning_prompts: Before you plot anything: where is zero on your line?
Which direction do you walk from 0 for a negative number, and how many steps?
-6 and -3: which one is farther FROM zero? So which one is farther left?
If I folded the number line at 0, where would 4 land? What number lives there?
What number is exactly halfway between -2 and -1?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student plots -6 to the right of -3, keeping counting order on the negative side.
misconception_redirects.say: Put your finger on 0. To plot -6, you walk LEFT 6 steps -- count them out loud. Now plot -3 the same way. Which number ended up farther left? The negative side is a mirror: bigger count, farther left.
misconception_redirects.praise: You counted from zero in the right direction -- that's exactly how the negative side works.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student counts ticks from the left END of the printed line instead of counting steps from 0.
misconception_redirects.say: The end of the picture is just where the paper stops -- it isn't a starting point. Zero is home base. Find 0 first, then count your steps from there.
misconception_redirects.praise: Starting at zero every time -- that habit will never let you down.

quick_checks.prompt: Sketch a quick number line and plot -4 and -1. Which is farther left?
quick_checks.look_for: -4 farther left. If -4 lands right of -1, the mirror misconception is live and S2 comparisons will fail too.

quick_checks.prompt: Point at -2.5 on this line (ticks every 0.5).
quick_checks.look_for: Lands between -3 and -2. Landing between -2 and -1 (counting magnitude toward zero) or at 2.5 (dropped sign) diagnoses which piece is missing.

worked_solution.stem: Plot -6 and -3 on a number line. Which one is farther left?

steps.annotation: Zero is home base. Every plot starts there, not at the end of the picture.
The negative sign means 'go left of zero.' Count the steps out loud: 1, 2, 3.
Six steps left is farther from zero than three steps left.
On the negative side, a bigger count means farther LEFT -- the mirror of the positive side.

faded_example.stem: Plot -5 and -2 on a number line. Which one is farther left?

steps.math: Find 0. Plot -2 by walking left 2 steps from 0.
steps.annotation: Zero first, then count left.
Now plot -5 the same way. How many steps left of 0?
Which number ended up farther left? Write your answer.

sentence_starters: I started at 0 and walked ___ steps to the ___.
___ is farther left because it is farther from 0 on the negative side.

skills.name: Compare two rational numbers and choose the true inequality
skills.i_do_script: We're comparing two numbers -- often one or both negative -- and writing the inequality that tells the truth. Watch me compare -8 and -3. My eyes want to say -8 is bigger because 8 beats 3 -- that's the trap. I sketch a quick number line instead: -8 is eight steps left of zero, -3 is only three steps left. -3 is farther RIGHT, so -3 is greater. I write -8 < -3 and read it out loud: 'negative eight is less than negative three.'

canonical_error.pattern: Compares the digits and ignores the signs -- decides -8 > -3 because 8 > 3
canonical_error.example: Student writes -8 > -3 and explains 'eight is bigger than three, so negative eight is bigger'
canonical_error.why: The student is comparing sizes (absolute values) instead of positions. They don't yet own that the negative sign flips the order: being 8 below zero is LESS than being 3 below zero, even though 8 is the bigger count.

redirect_script.stop: Wait -- check the number line before you trust the digits.
redirect_script.prompt: Sketch a quick line and plot both numbers. -8 is eight steps LEFT of zero; -3 is only three steps left. Which one is farther right? Farther right always wins. Now write the symbol so the sentence tells the truth.
redirect_script.praise: You checked position instead of digit size -- that's the move that beats this trap every time.

skills.item_template: Two rational numbers, usually in a real-world context (temperature, elevation, money). Student selects or writes the inequality that correctly compares them. MC with 4 inequality choices, or NR.

sample_items.stem: The average temperature on the planet Mercury is 333 degrees F. The average temperature on the planet Neptune is -330 degrees F. Which inequality compares the two temperatures?
sample_items.distractor_logic: '-330 > 333' and '333 < -330' bait students who see 330 and 333 as nearly equal digits and ignore the sign; '=' baits 'they're about the same size'

sample_items.stem: The temperature in the morning was -5 degrees F. By afternoon it was 12 degrees F. Which inequality correctly compares the two temperatures?
sample_items.distractor_logic: '-5 > 12' baits reading the negative as 'a big cold number'; '12 < -5' is the same error written the other way

sample_items.stem: Which inequality is true?
sample_items.distractor_logic: '-8 > -3' is the canonical magnitude error (8 > 3); '-3 < -8' is the same bug with the numbers swapped

sample_items.stem: The lowest point in Death Valley is at an elevation of -282 feet. Denver sits at an elevation of 5280 feet. Which inequality compares the two elevations?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Distractors bait students who treat 'deeper' or 'more extreme' as 'greater'

vocabulary.definition: Any number that can be written as a fraction of two integers -- includes integers, fractions, decimals, and their negatives.
A math sentence that uses < or > to say one value is less than or greater than another.
How much a number is worth -- decided by its position on the number line, not by how big its digits look.
Height compared to sea level. Above sea level is positive; below sea level is negative.

next_steps.if_pass: Move to 6NS3-S3: judge whole statements of order as true or false across a table of values.
next_steps.if_fail: Drop back to 6NS3-S1 -- if the student can't place -8 left of -3, the comparison has nothing to stand on.

worked_example_script.text: Write on the board: 'Which is greater: -8 or -3?' Underneath, write the tempting claim: '-8, because 8 is bigger than 3.'
A lot of smart students agree with that claim. What is it actually comparing -- the numbers, or something about the numbers?
Draw a number line from -10 to 2. Plot -8 and -3.
Which mark is farther to the right? What does 'farther right' always mean on a number line?
Try it with money: one account is at -8 dollars, another at -3 dollars. Which account is in better shape?
So which symbol goes between them: -8 __ -3? Read your finished statement out loud like a sentence.
If the student writes > or reads the sentence and shrugs, go back to the line: 'Point at the greater one. Is it on the left or the right? Does your symbol agree with your finger?'
Digits measure size; the number line measures value. When signs are involved, trust the line: -8 < -3.

practice_problems.stem: Write < or >: -6 __ 2
Which is greater: -1 or -7?
Write < or >: -8 __ -3
practice_problems.notes: The trap head-on. Expect > from digit-comparers; send them to the number line.

practice_problems.stem: The temperature on Monday was -9 degrees F. On Tuesday it was -4 degrees F. Which inequality correctly compares the two temperatures?
practice_problems.notes: Both negative AND in context -- 'colder' must map to 'less.'

practice_problems.stem: Tia compared -8 and -3. Find her mistake and fix it.
shown_work: Tia said: '8 is bigger than 3, so -8 is bigger than -3.'
practice_problems.answer: -8 < -3. Tia compared the digits, but the negative sign flips the order: -8 is eight steps LEFT of zero and -3 is only three steps left, so -3 is farther right and greater. Being 8 dollars in debt is worse than being 3 dollars in debt.
practice_problems.notes: The canonical magnitude error with fresh framing.

practice_problems.stem: Plot -5 and -1 on the number line. Circle the greater number.
practice_problems.answer: -1 (it is farther right)

practice_problems.stem: Write a number that makes this statement true: -4 < __ < 0
practice_problems.answer: Any number between -4 and 0, such as -2
practice_problems.notes: Producing a number between two negatives shows real position sense.

practice_problems.stem: Is 0 greater than EVERY negative number? Explain using the number line.
practice_problems.answer: Yes. Every negative number sits to the left of 0, and farther right is always greater, so 0 is greater than every negative number.
practice_problems.notes: Explain-why stretch: the zero boundary in words.

activities.title: Tia's Trap
activities.instructions:
1. Show Tia's claim that -8 > -3 and let the group react before you say anything.
2. Ask: what was Tia thinking? (Her rule works perfectly for positive numbers -- that's why it's sticky.)
3. Each student proves the fix two ways: a quick number line, and a money story (owing $8 vs owing $3).
4. Each student writes Tia a one-sentence tip that does NOT use the word 'bigger.'

content.worked_problem: Compare -8 and -3. Tia wrote: -8 > -3, because 8 is bigger than 3.
content.error_step: Tia compared the digit sizes and ignored what the negative sign does to order.
content.why: The negative sign flips the order: -8 is farther below zero than -3, so it is LESS. On the number line -8 sits left of -3, and left means less.

activities.title: True or Trap?
materials: Two header cards: TRUE and FALSE
activities.instructions:
1. Lay the TRUE and FALSE headers on the desk.
2. Partners take turns drawing an inequality card, reading it out loud as a sentence, and sorting it.
3. The partner must agree or challenge; a challenge means both sketch the number line before checking.
4. Debrief: every FALSE card here is false for the same reason -- what is it?

activities.title: Inequality Showdown
materials: Deck of integer cards from -12 to 12
activities.instructions:
1. Each partner flips one card face up.
2. Both race to write the true inequality comparing the two cards (like -7 < 4).
3. First correct statement read ALOUD as a sentence earns the point -- a statement written but misread earns nothing.
4. Any negative-negative pair (like -7 and -2) is worth double, because that's where the trap lives.
5. Play to 10. Debrief: which pairs of cards caused wrong answers, and what did they have in common?

strategy_links.why: The '-8 > -3 because 8 > 3' bug is the single most analyzable error in the standard -- put it under the microscope.
Short number talks ('which is greater, -8 or -3, and how do you SEE it?') surface digit-comparing reasoning out loud where it can be fixed.
Whiteboard rounds of two-number comparisons reveal instantly who is still comparing digit sizes.

questioning_prompts: Which of these two numbers is farther RIGHT on the number line?
You said 8 is bigger than 3 -- true! But what does the negative sign do to that comparison?
Would you rather owe $8 or owe $3? Which account balance is greater, -8 or -3?
Which is colder, -9 degrees or -4 degrees? So which number is LESS?
Read your inequality out loud as a sentence. Does the sentence tell the truth?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student writes -8 > -3 and justifies it with '8 is bigger than 3.'
misconception_redirects.say: Sketch a quick line and plot both numbers. -8 is eight steps LEFT of zero; -3 is only three steps left. Which one is farther right? Farther right always wins. Now write the symbol so the sentence tells the truth.
misconception_redirects.praise: You checked position instead of digit size -- that's the move that beats this trap every time.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student flips the symbol direction -- knows -3 is greater but writes -3 < -8.
misconception_redirects.say: Read your statement out loud, left to right: 'negative three is less than negative eight.' Is that the sentence you meant to say? Flip the symbol until the spoken sentence matches what you know.
misconception_redirects.praise: You made the symbol say exactly what you meant -- comparison right, sentence right.

quick_checks.look_for: Instant thumbs down. A thumbs up means digit-comparison is still running; hesitation means the number line isn't automatic yet.

quick_checks.prompt: Write the true inequality for -6 and -9, then say it as a money sentence.
quick_checks.look_for: -9 < -6 (or -6 > -9) plus something like 'owing $9 is worse than owing $6.' A student who can't produce the story is leaning on a memorized rule.

worked_solution.stem: Which is greater, -8 or -3? Write the true inequality.

steps.math: Trap check: 8 > 3, but these are NEGATIVE numbers.
steps.annotation: Digit size is not value. The negative sign flips the order.

steps.math: Plot both: -8 is 8 steps left of 0; -3 is 3 steps left of 0.
steps.annotation: A quick sketch settles it -- position is what 'greater' actually means.

steps.math: -3 is farther right, so -3 is greater.
steps.annotation: Farther right always wins, on every number line.
Read it out loud: 'negative eight is less than negative three.' The sentence tells the truth.

faded_example.stem: Which is greater, -7 or -2? Write the true inequality.

steps.math: Plot both numbers: -7 is 7 steps left of 0; -2 is 2 steps left of 0.
steps.annotation: Position first -- never trust the digits alone.
Which number is farther right? That one is greater.
Write the inequality and read it out loud to check.

sentence_starters: ___ is greater because it is farther to the RIGHT on the number line.
The digits say ___, but the negative sign flips the order, so ___.

skills.name: Evaluate statements of order about a set of rational numbers
skills.i_do_script: Now someone ELSE writes the comparison and our job is to judge it: true or false. Watch me check the statement '-15 > 12' from a game-score table. I don't ask 'which digits are bigger?' -- I ask 'where do these live on the number line?' -15 is below zero, 12 is above zero, and anything below zero is less than anything above it. The statement claims the opposite, so it's FALSE. One statement at a time, position check, verdict.

canonical_error.pattern: Judges a statement by comparing sizes -- accepts '-15 > 12' as true because 15 > 12
canonical_error.example: Given a table where Bo has -25 points and Dee has 30, the student marks 'Bo's points > Dee's points' as TRUE because 25 looks close to 30 and 'negative just means he lost them'
canonical_error.why: Same root as the comparison bug, but hidden one layer deeper: when the numbers arrive inside a table and a ready-made claim, the student verifies the DIGITS of the claim instead of re-deriving the comparison from position. The negative sign gets processed as a label ('lost points') instead of as a value.

redirect_script.stop: Don't grade the claim yet -- find the two numbers first.
redirect_script.prompt: Pull the two values out of the table and write them side by side. Now ask the only question that matters: which one is farther right on the number line? Then check whether the statement agrees with you.
redirect_script.praise: You re-did the comparison yourself instead of trusting the claim -- that's how you catch false statements.

skills.item_template: A table of named values (game points, temperatures, balances) with positive and negative entries, plus one or more comparison statements. Student decides which statement is true, or judges one statement true/false. MC or T/F.

sample_items.stem: A group of friends are playing a game. Players can gain or lose points. Each player's total is given in the table. Which comparison statement is TRUE?
sample_items.distractor_logic: '-25 > 30' baits size-comparison plus 'negative is just a label'; '-4 > 18' baits the same; '=' baits students who compare loosely

sample_items.stem: Determine whether the statement is true or false: -12 > 4
sample_items.distractor_logic: 12 > 4 in digits -- the whole item is the magnitude bait

sample_items.stem: The table shows the low temperature in four cities on the same day. Determine whether this statement is true or false: Fargo's temperature < Duluth's temperature.
sample_items.distractor_logic: -19 vs -11: digit-comparers call -19 the 'bigger cold' and mark false

sample_items.stem: The table shows the change in four bank accounts this week. Which statement is TRUE?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Every distractor is a magnitude comparison that ignores signs -- 40.50 vs 12.75, 8.25 vs 0, 12.75 vs 8.25

vocabulary.definition: Decide which of two values is greater, which is less, or whether they are equal.
Money put INTO an account -- a positive change.
Money taken OUT of an account -- a negative change.
A claim about which values are greater or less, like '-25 < -4.' It can be true or false -- your job is to check it.

next_steps.if_pass: Move to 6NS3-S4: order a whole list of rational numbers, not just judge one pair.
next_steps.if_fail: Return to 6NS3-S2 with the same table values as bare pairs -- if the student can compare -25 and -4 alone but not inside the table, practice extracting values first.

worked_example_script.text: Post a small table: Ana 18, Bo -25, Cam -4, Dee 30 (game points). Below it write the claim: 'Bo's points > Cam's points.'
Someone is claiming something about Bo and Cam. Before we judge it -- what are Bo's points, and what are Cam's? Point to each in the table.
Write the two values side by side: -25 and -4.
Forget the claim for a second. YOU compare them: which of -25 and -4 is farther right on a number line?
If the student says -25 is greater 'because 25 beats 4,' have them sketch the line and plot both before continuing. The claim can't be judged until their own comparison is solid.
So your comparison says -4 > -25. Now bring the claim back: it says Bo > Cam, meaning -25 > -4. Does the claim agree with you or disagree?
What's the verdict -- true or false? And what's the one-sentence reason you'd give?
That's the whole routine: pull the values, do YOUR OWN comparison, then grade the claim last. Never grade a claim you haven't re-done yourself.

practice_problems.stem: True or false: 5 > -12
practice_problems.answer: True

practice_problems.stem: True or false: -3 < -1
practice_problems.answer: True

practice_problems.stem: The table shows players' points: Ana 18, Bo -25, Cam -4, Dee 30. Which statement is TRUE: (a) -25 > 30, (b) -25 < -4, (c) -4 > 18?
practice_problems.notes: Both wrong choices are magnitude comparisons in disguise.

practice_problems.stem: True or false: -25 > 14. Explain your answer in one sentence.
practice_problems.answer: False. Every negative number is less than every positive number, so -25 < 14.
practice_problems.notes: Requires the one-sentence justification -- rehearsal for S6.

practice_problems.stem: Marco judged the statement below. Find his mistake and fix it.
shown_work: Marco said: '15 is bigger than 12, so -15 is bigger than 12.'
practice_problems.answer: False. Marco compared digit sizes, but -15 is below zero and 12 is above zero. Every number below zero is less than every number above it, so -15 < 12.
practice_problems.notes: The canonical magnitude error inside a true/false judgment.

practice_problems.stem: Plot -15 and 12 on the number line. Then write TRUE or FALSE for the statement '-15 > 12.'
practice_problems.answer: False (-15 is far to the left of 12)

practice_problems.stem: Write a TRUE comparison statement using the numbers -6 and -13.
practice_problems.notes: Producing a true statement instead of judging one -- the bridge to S5.

practice_problems.stem: Kai says '0 > -8' and '-8 < 0' are the same statement. Is he right? Explain.
practice_problems.answer: Yes. Swapping the two sides AND flipping the symbol keeps the same meaning -- both say -8 is the smaller number.
practice_problems.notes: Symbol flexibility -- both directions must read as one fact.

activities.title: Statement Court
materials: A projected or printed data table of six players' points
activities.instructions:
1. Post the table: Ana 18, Bo -25, Cam -4, Dee 30, Eli 0, Fay -17.
2. Groups sort the 12 statement cards into TRUE and FALSE.
3. Rule: a card can only be placed after someone reads the two values it uses straight from the table.
4. Debrief on the two or three cards groups disagreed about -- almost always negative-negative comparisons.

activities.title: Marco's Verdict
activities.instructions:
1. Pairs read Marco's 'True' verdict on '-15 > 12' and identify his exact reasoning step.
2. Ask: when WOULD Marco's rule work? (Only when both numbers are positive.)
3. Pairs write the correct verdict plus a one-sentence rule that survives negatives.
4. Debrief question: what should you check FIRST before comparing any two numbers?

content.worked_problem: Statement: -15 > 12. Marco wrote: True, because 15 is bigger than 12.
content.error_step: Marco verified the digits of the claim instead of checking positions -- the negative sign never entered his decision.
content.why: -15 is below zero and 12 is above zero. Any number below zero is less than any number above zero, so -15 < 12 and the statement is false.

activities.title: Fact or Fib Rapid Fire
activities.instructions:
1. Read a statement aloud ('negative twenty is greater than negative six').
2. On 'show,' every student signals TRUE or FALSE at once.
3. When the room splits, have one student from each side defend their verdict in one sentence before revealing.
4. Keep a tally: statements with two negatives should appear at least five times -- that's where the splits happen.

strategy_links.why: Think-Pair-Share fits verdict work: private verdict, partner defense, then whole-group ruling on the contested statements.
Judging a worked (wrong) comparison like Marco's IS this skill -- the strategy and the content are the same move.
Choral true/false rounds build fast, automatic position-checking on high-frequency comparisons.

questioning_prompts: Which two values does this statement actually use? Point to them in the table.
Before you grade the claim: which of those two numbers is farther right on the number line?
Does the statement agree with YOUR comparison, or disagree?
This player has negative points -- is that a label, or a value? What does it mean for the comparison?
Can a statement with a bigger-looking number on the left still be false? Give me an example.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student marks '-15 > 12' true, reasoning that 15 beats 12.
misconception_redirects.say: Pull the two values out of the table and write them side by side. Now ask the only question that matters: which one is farther right on the number line? Then check whether the statement agrees with you.
misconception_redirects.praise: You re-did the comparison yourself instead of trusting the claim -- that's how you catch false statements.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student grades statements about the wrong rows -- grabs Ana's value when the claim names Bo.
misconception_redirects.say: Underline the two names in the statement, then trace each name across its table row with your finger before you copy the value. Names first, numbers second.
misconception_redirects.praise: You matched every name to its own value -- the comparison can't go wrong before it starts now.

quick_checks.look_for: False, fast. 'True' means magnitude comparison is still deciding; slow correct answers mean the number line isn't automatic.

quick_checks.prompt: Make up one FALSE statement about these values: 7, -3, -11. Then tell me why it's false.
quick_checks.look_for: A deliberately false claim plus a position-based reason. Students who can only produce true statements aren't yet standing outside the claim to judge it.

worked_solution.stem: The table shows each player's points. True or false: Bo's points > Cam's points.

steps.annotation: Get the two numbers out of the table before judging anything.

steps.math: Position check: -25 is 25 steps left of 0; -4 is 4 steps left.
steps.annotation: Don't compare 25 and 4 -- compare positions.
Cam's total is greater, even though Bo's number has bigger digits.

steps.math: The claim says Bo > Cam. Verdict: FALSE.
steps.annotation: Compare your result to the claim last -- that's the actual true/false decision.

faded_example.stem: The table shows each player's points. True or false: Fay's points > Eli's points.

steps.annotation: Values out of the table first.
Which value is farther right on the number line -- -17 or 0?
Does the claim agree with your comparison? Write TRUE or FALSE.

sentence_starters: The statement is ___ because ___ is farther to the ___ on the number line.
I checked the claim by comparing ___ and ___ myself first.

skills.name: Order rational numbers from least to greatest or greatest to least
skills.i_do_script: Now we line up a whole list -- fractions, decimals, and negatives mixed together. Watch me order -3/4, 0.5, -0.7, and 1/4 from least to greatest. First I put everything in one costume: -3/4 = -0.75 and 1/4 = 0.25. Then I place them on a number line in my head: the negatives go left of zero, and between -0.75 and -0.7, the -0.75 is farther left. So: -3/4, -0.7, 1/4, 0.5. Convert first, position second -- and remember the negative side runs backwards.

canonical_error.pattern: Orders the negative numbers by their size -- writes -1.35 before -1.75 going 'up' because 1.35 < 1.75
canonical_error.example: Asked for least to greatest with -1.75, -1.5, -1.35, the student writes -1.35, -1.5, -1.75 because '1.35 is the smallest'
canonical_error.why: The student converts correctly and orders the sizes correctly -- then forgets that the negative side of the number line runs in reverse. The bigger the distance below zero, the SMALLER the value, so a correct positive-ordering habit produces an exactly backwards negative ordering.

redirect_script.stop: Pause -- did the negative side flip on you?
redirect_script.prompt: Sketch the number line and actually plot each negative number. -1.75 lands farther left than -1.35, doesn't it? Least to greatest means reading left to right off YOUR line -- not smallest digits first.
redirect_script.praise: You plotted before you ordered -- the line caught the flip for you.

skills.item_template: A list of 3-5 rational numbers mixing fractions, decimals, mixed numbers, and negatives -- often close in value. Student orders least to greatest or greatest to least (NR), or selects the correctly ordered list (MC).

sample_items.stem: Order the following numbers from least to greatest: -3/4, 0.5, -0.7, 1/4
sample_items.distractor_logic: -0.7 vs -3/4 = -0.75 is the pinch point: size-orderers put -0.7 first because 0.7 < 0.75

sample_items.stem: Select the list that shows the numbers ordered from greatest to least.
sample_items.distractor_logic: '22/6, 4, ...' misorders 22/6 (about 3.67) above 4; the others are least-to-greatest or magnitude orderings

sample_items.stem: Order the following numbers from least to greatest: -1.35, -1 1/2, -1 1/4, -1.75
sample_items.distractor_logic: All four share the leading digit -- size-ordering gives the exactly reversed list

sample_items.stem: Order the following numbers from least to greatest: 0.8, 3/4, 0.09, 7/8
sample_items.distractor_logic: 0.09 baits 'two digits beats one digit'; 3/4 vs 0.8 requires converting to 0.75

vocabulary.definition: Arrange numbers by value -- least to greatest reads left to right on the number line; greatest to least reads right to left.
The smallest value -- the one farthest LEFT on a horizontal number line.
The largest value -- the one farthest RIGHT on a horizontal number line.
A whole number and a fraction together, like -2 1/4, which means 2 and a quarter below zero: -2.25.

next_steps.if_pass: Move to 6NS3-S5: write your own inequality statements from real-world situations.
next_steps.if_fail: If conversions (3/4 = 0.75) are the failure point, rebuild with 6NS3-F2. If conversions are fine but negatives come out reversed, replay 6NS3-S2's number-line check on pairs pulled from the list.

worked_example_script.text: Write on the board: 'Order from least to greatest: -3/4, 0.5, -0.7, 1/4.'
These numbers are wearing different costumes -- fractions and decimals mixed. What could we do first so they're all easy to compare?
Convert with me: what is -3/4 as a decimal? And 1/4?
Rewrite the list: -0.75, 0.5, -0.7, 0.25. Then draw a number line from -1 to 1 with ticks every 0.25.
Sort first by side of zero: which of these live on the left of 0? Now, between -0.75 and -0.7, which is farther from zero -- and so which is farther LEFT?
If the student puts -0.7 left of -0.75 ('7 is less than 75'), have them plot both between -1 and 0 and look. The line settles it.
Read the four plotted points left to right. What's the order, back in their original costumes?
Convert first, plot second, read left to right -- and remember: on the negative side, the ordering of the sizes flips.

practice_problems.stem: Order from least to greatest: 7, -3, 0
Order from least to greatest: -2, -9, 4
Order from least to greatest: -1.4, 0.75, -0.9, 1/2
practice_problems.notes: 1/2 = 0.5 must slot below 0.75 -- conversion plus the negative flip in one item.

practice_problems.stem: Order from greatest to least: -5/2, -2.09, -2 3/4
practice_problems.notes: All three between -2 and -3. Convert: -5/2 = -2.5, -2 3/4 = -2.75. Greatest = closest to zero.

practice_problems.stem: Lena ordered three numbers from least to greatest. Find her mistake and fix it.
shown_work: Lena said: '0.25 is less than 0.5, and 0.5 is less than 0.8, so I kept that order.'
practice_problems.answer: -0.8, -0.5, -0.25. Lena ordered the sizes, but these are negatives -- the number farthest below zero is the LEAST. -0.8 is farthest left on the number line, so it comes first.
practice_problems.notes: The canonical error: a perfect positive ordering, exactly backwards for negatives.

practice_problems.stem: Plot -1.5, -0.5, and 1 on the number line. Which number is least?
Order from least to greatest: -1 2/5, -1.3, -1.45
practice_problems.notes: -1 2/5 = -1.4 sits between the other two. Same leading digits -- the spec's hardest tier.

practice_problems.stem: Write three different numbers between -2 and -1, then order YOUR numbers from least to greatest.
practice_problems.answer: Any three numbers between -2 and -1 in increasing order, such as -1.9, -1.5, -1.1
practice_problems.notes: Produce-your-own stretch: students must generate and then self-order.

activities.title: Human Number Line
materials: A wall or whiteboard ledge as the line
activities.instructions:
1. Hand out one card per student (extras double up as judges).
2. Students arrange themselves least to greatest WITHOUT talking -- gestures only.
3. Judges then interview neighbors: 'Convince me you two are in the right order.' Any pair that can't justify swaps or defends until the room agrees.
4. Debrief: which two cards took longest to settle, and why were they both negative?

activities.title: Lena's Backwards List
activities.instructions:
1. Pairs read Lena's ordering of -0.8, -0.25, -0.5 and find what she did RIGHT (her size comparisons are all correct).
2. Then they plot all three on the strip and read least to greatest off the line.
3. Ask: why did correct size-ordering produce an exactly backwards answer?
4. Each pair writes a one-line rule for ordering negatives that Lena could tape to her desk.

content.worked_problem: Order from least to greatest: -0.8, -0.25, -0.5. Lena wrote: -0.25, -0.5, -0.8.
content.error_step: Lena ordered the distances from zero (0.25 < 0.5 < 0.8) and kept that order for the negative values.
content.why: On the negative side, MORE distance below zero means LESS value. The correct order is the exact reverse: -0.8 < -0.5 < -0.25.

activities.title: Order Up!
materials: Deck of 24 rational-number cards (fractions, decimals, mixed numbers, half of them negative)
activities.instructions:
1. Deal each group 4 cards face up.
2. On 'go,' the group arranges its cards least to greatest; first correct group scores 2 points.
3. Groups check each other -- a successful challenge steals the points.
4. Each round, swap one card in for a new draw. After five rounds, ask which single card caused the most rearranging (usually a negative fraction like -3/4).

strategy_links.why: Physical card lines and drawn number lines before symbol-only ordering -- CRA carries the negative flip from felt to abstract.
Lena's reversed list is the standard's most instructive wrong answer -- correct reasoning, wrong side of zero.
Ordering close negatives sparks genuine disagreement, and Think-Pair-Share makes each student commit to a position before consensus.

questioning_prompts: Which of these numbers can you rewrite so everything wears the same costume -- all decimals or all fractions?
Where does each number live: left of zero or right of zero? Sort that first.
Between -1.75 and -1.35, which is farther from zero? So which is LESS?
You ordered the positives correctly -- does the same left-to-right habit work on the negative side? Why not?
Read your finished list off a number line: does it actually run left to right?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student's negatives come out exactly backwards -- -1.35 listed before -1.75 for 'least to greatest.'
misconception_redirects.say: Sketch the number line and actually plot each negative number. -1.75 lands farther left than -1.35, doesn't it? Least to greatest means reading left to right off YOUR line -- not smallest digits first.
misconception_redirects.praise: You plotted before you ordered -- the line caught the flip for you.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student compares 3/4 and 0.8 without converting, or guesses that 22/6 is bigger than 4.
misconception_redirects.say: Put every number in the same costume first: 3/4 becomes 0.75, 22/6 becomes about 3.67. You can't line up numbers that are speaking different languages.
misconception_redirects.praise: Converting first made every comparison easy -- that's the pro move.

quick_checks.prompt: Order -0.5, -0.9, -0.2 from least to greatest, out loud, in ten seconds.
quick_checks.look_for: -0.9, -0.5, -0.2. The reversed list (-0.2 first) means the negative flip isn't automatic; hesitation on all three means conversions are eating working memory.

quick_checks.prompt: Which is greater: -2 1/4 or -2.4? One sentence of proof.
quick_checks.look_for: -2 1/4 (= -2.25) is greater because it is closer to zero. Watch for '2.4 > 2.25 so -2.4 is greater' -- the magnitude bug resurfacing under conversion load.

steps.annotation: Convert every fraction to a decimal so all four numbers speak the same language.

steps.math: All four are negative: plot -1.75, -1.5, -1.35, -1.25 left of zero.
steps.annotation: The farthest below zero (-1.75) sits farthest LEFT.
Least to greatest is just the left-to-right reading off the line.
Switch back to each number's original costume for the final answer.
Convert the fraction to a decimal first.
Plot -0.75, -0.6, and 0.3 on a quick number line. Which is farthest left?
Read the line left to right and write the order using the original forms.

sentence_starters: I converted ___ to ___ so every number wore the same costume.
___ is least because it is farthest below zero.

skills.name: Write and interpret inequality statements in real-world contexts
skills.i_do_script: Now WE write the inequality -- nobody hands us choices. Watch me with this one: 'On a horizontal number line, -8.25 is to the left of -6.34. Write an inequality.' The words 'to the left of' are doing all the work: left means LESS, every time, on every horizontal line. So I write -8.25 < -6.34 and read it back: 'negative 8.25 is less than negative 6.34.' Same move with stories: a diver at -35 feet is lower than one at -6 feet, so -35 < -6.

canonical_error.pattern: Writes the symbol from word order or context drama instead of position -- 'to the left of' or 'first-mentioned' becomes >
canonical_error.example: Given '-8.25 is to the left of -6.34,' the student writes -8.25 > -6.34 because -8.25 was named first (or because 8.25 'sounds bigger')
canonical_error.why: The student hasn't welded the positional words to value: LEFT means less, RIGHT means greater, LOWER (elevation) means less, COLDER means less. Without that anchor, they fall back on sentence order or digit size to pick the symbol.

redirect_script.stop: Stop -- what does 'to the left of' mean for VALUE?
redirect_script.prompt: Draw the line and put both numbers where the sentence says they are. The one on the left is less -- so its symbol is <. Now read your inequality out loud and check it against the picture.
redirect_script.praise: You turned the position words into the right symbol -- that's exactly what this standard asks for.

skills.item_template: A real-world situation (elevation, banking, temperature, money) or a positional statement ('x is to the left of y'), sometimes with a data table. Student writes the inequality (NR), or interprets what a given inequality means in context (MC).

sample_items.stem: On a horizontal number line, -8.25 is to the left of -6.34. Write an inequality to represent this statement.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Common error: -8.25 > -6.34 from 'named first' or digit size

sample_items.stem: On a horizontal number line, -2 is to the right of -5. Write an inequality to represent this statement.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Common error: -2 < -5 because 2 < 5

sample_items.stem: Penny tracks her bank account. The table shows her balance at the end of each month. Write an inequality that compares Penny's highest monthly balance with her lowest monthly balance.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Students may pick 12.50 as highest (first big number seen) or -4.82 as 'highest' because 4.82 is not the biggest digit string

sample_items.stem: A hiker records her elevation at four stops along a trail. Write an inequality that compares the hiker's highest elevation with her lowest elevation.
sample_items.distractor_logic: The lowest value is negative -- students hunting for 'the smallest digits' pick 78

sample_items.stem: The overnight low in Fairbanks was -15 degrees F. The overnight low in Indianapolis was 28 degrees F. Write an inequality that compares the two temperatures.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Common error: -15 > 28 because 'negative 15 is a more extreme temperature'

sample_items.stem: A debit changes Theo's account by -12 dollars. A credit changes it by 9 dollars. Write an inequality that compares the two changes.
sample_items.distractor_logic: The debit has bigger digits -- magnitude-comparers write -12 > 9

sample_items.stem: Two divers are underwater. The inequality -50 < -20 compares their elevations in feet. What does this statement mean?
sample_items.answer: The diver at -50 feet is deeper below sea level than the diver at -20 feet
choices: The diver at -50 feet is deeper below sea level than the diver at -20 feet
The diver at -50 feet is closer to the surface than the diver at -20 feet
The diver at -20 feet is deeper below sea level than the diver at -50 feet
The two divers are at the same depth
sample_items.distractor_logic: Interpretation reversal: students who read < as 'smaller digits' pick the closer-to-surface option

sample_items.stem: On a horizontal number line, 0 is to the right of -3.5. Write an inequality to represent this statement.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Common error: treating 0 as 'nothing' and writing 0 < -3.5

sample_items.stem: A submarine is at an elevation of -275 feet. A whale is swimming at -180 feet. Write an inequality that compares the two elevations.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Both negative: 275 > 180 in digits baits -275 > -180

sample_items.stem: The inequality -4 > -9 compares two overnight temperatures in degrees F. Which temperature is warmer?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Students who map 'bigger digits' to 'more heat' answer -9

sample_items.stem: On a vertical number line, like a thermometer, -3 is above -7. Write an inequality to represent this statement.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Vertical orientation: above means greater; digit-comparers write -3 < -7

vocabulary.definition: Running side to side, like the floor. On a horizontal number line, right means greater.
Running up and down, like a thermometer. On a vertical number line, up means greater.
The zero of elevation. Heights above it are positive; depths below it are negative.
Height above sea level -- another word for how high something is.
Say what a math statement means in the real situation -- turn -50 < -20 back into words about divers or dollars.

next_steps.if_pass: Move to 6NS3-S6: defend and explain comparisons of very close rational numbers.
next_steps.if_fail: Return to 6NS3-S2 to re-anchor left/right = less/greater with bare numbers, then re-attach the context words (lower, colder, deeper, owes more) one at a time.

worked_example_script.text: Write on the board: 'On a horizontal number line, -8.25 is to the left of -6.34. Write an inequality to represent this statement.'
No answer choices this time -- we write it ourselves. Which words in that sentence are the math-y ones, the ones doing the work?
'To the left of' -- on a horizontal number line, what does being on the left always mean about a number's value?
Sketch a quick line, place -8.25 on the left and -6.34 to its right, exactly as the sentence says.
So which of the two numbers is LESS? Which symbol says 'is less than'?
If the student writes -8.25 > -6.34 'because it came first' or 'because 8.25 is bigger,' point at the sketch: 'Which mark is on the left? What did we say left means?'
Write the inequality and read it out loud. Could you also write it the other way around and still tell the truth? How?
Position words pick the symbol: left, lower, colder, deeper all mean LESS. -8.25 < -6.34, or equally -6.34 > -8.25.

practice_problems.stem: On a horizontal number line, -4 is to the left of 1. Write an inequality to represent this statement.
Which is warmer: -12 degrees F or -2 degrees F?
practice_problems.answer: -2 degrees F

practice_problems.stem: A scuba diver is at -35 feet. A snorkeler is at -6 feet. Write an inequality that compares the two elevations.
practice_problems.notes: Both negative in context. Watch for -35 > -6 justified by 'deeper is more.'

practice_problems.stem: The table shows Mara's account balance at the end of each month: January 15.20, February -8.45, March 3.10, April -2.60 (dollars). Write an inequality comparing her lowest balance with her highest balance.
practice_problems.notes: Two negatives in the table -- the lowest is -8.45, not -2.60.

practice_problems.stem: Jo wrote an inequality for a positional statement. Find her mistake and fix it.
shown_work: Statement: on a horizontal number line, -7.5 is to the left of -3.
Jo said: '-7.5 came first in the sentence, and 7.5 is bigger than 3.'
practice_problems.answer: -7.5 < -3. 'To the left of' means LESS on a horizontal number line -- sentence order and digit size have nothing to do with it. Left is less, every time.
practice_problems.notes: Baits both halves of the canonical error: word order and magnitude.

practice_problems.stem: Plot -7.5 and -3 on the number line. Then write the inequality that the picture shows.
Write a real-world sentence about money, temperature, or elevation that matches the inequality -15 < -5.
practice_problems.answer: Any correct context, such as: 'Owing $15 leaves you with less money than owing $5' or 'A temperature of -15 degrees is colder than -5 degrees.'
practice_problems.notes: Reverse direction: from symbols to story. Recognition isn't ownership.

practice_problems.stem: On a vertical thermometer, -2 is above -10. Write the inequality, and explain which direction means greater on a vertical number line.
practice_problems.answer: -2 > -10. On a vertical number line, UP means greater -- above always beats below.
practice_problems.notes: Transfers the left/right anchor to up/down, which the spec's vocabulary list expects.

activities.title: Story-Symbol Match
materials: 8 story cards and 10 inequality cards (two decoys)
activities.instructions:
1. Spread all cards face up.
2. Partners match each real-world story to its inequality -- two inequality cards are decoys with flipped symbols.
3. Rule: before placing a match, the reader must say which value is greater IN THE STORY (warmer, higher, more money).
4. Debrief: which story almost got a decoy, and which single word decided it?

pairs.left: A diver at -35 ft is deeper than a diver at -6 ft
Fairbanks at -15 degrees was colder than Indy at 28 degrees
A balance of 20.34 dollars beats a balance of -4.82 dollars
The trail's high point 316 ft tops its low point -20 ft
-2 sits to the right of -5 on a number line
A debit of -12 dollars is less than a credit of 9 dollars
A whale at -180 ft is above a sub at -275 ft
-8.25 sits to the left of -6.34 on a number line

activities.title: Jo's Word-Order Trap
activities.instructions:
1. Groups read Jo's inequality for '-7.5 is to the left of -3' and name BOTH things that steered her wrong (sentence order and digit size).
2. Each student plots the two numbers and reads the true statement off the line.
3. Groups write the one anchor rule Jo needs ('left = less').
4. Debrief: does 'named first in the sentence' EVER decide the symbol? (No -- only position does.)

content.worked_problem: Statement: -7.5 is to the left of -3. Jo wrote: -7.5 > -3, because it came first and 7.5 is bigger than 3.
content.error_step: Jo picked the symbol from sentence order and digit size instead of from position.
content.why: On a horizontal number line, 'to the left of' means LESS -- always. -7.5 < -3.

activities.title: Context Dial: Money, Weather, Depth
activities.instructions:
1. At each station, students draw two value slips (like -8.45 and 3.10 at the bank station).
2. They write the inequality AND say it in the station's language: 'a balance of -8.45 dollars is less than 3.10 dollars.'
3. The thermometer station uses a VERTICAL line taped to the wall -- above means greater.
4. Rotate every 4 minutes. Debrief: what did 'less than' sound like at each station? (Owes more, colder, deeper.)

strategy_links.why: Thinking aloud -- 'left means less, so the symbol must be <' -- models the word-to-symbol anchor this skill lives on.
Model one context, write one together, release: gradual release fits the first skill where students produce inequalities on their own.
Jo's word-order error shows students exactly which cue (position, not sentence order) is allowed to pick the symbol.

questioning_prompts: In this story, which value is greater -- and which real-world word told you (warmer, higher, more money)?
'To the left of' -- what does that always mean for value on a horizontal line?
This line is vertical, like a thermometer. Which direction means greater now?
Before you write the symbol: say the true sentence out loud. Now make the symbol say it.
Your inequality is written -- read it BACKWARDS too ('-6.34 is greater than -8.25'). Do both readings match the story?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student writes > because a number was named first in the sentence, or because its digits are bigger.
misconception_redirects.say: Draw the line and put both numbers where the sentence says they are. The one on the left is less -- so its symbol is <. Now read your inequality out loud and check it against the picture.
misconception_redirects.praise: You turned the position words into the right symbol -- that's exactly what this standard asks for.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student picks the wrong 'lowest' value from a table -- chooses -2.60 over -8.45 because 2.60 has smaller digits.
misconception_redirects.say: Circle every negative value in the table, then plot just those on a quick line. The lowest balance is the one farthest LEFT -- which one is it?
misconception_redirects.praise: You found the true lowest by position -- tables can't trick you now.

quick_checks.prompt: Quick-write: '-30 is to the left of -12' as an inequality.
quick_checks.look_for: -30 < -12 within seconds. A > answer means word order or magnitude is still choosing the symbol.
Something like '5 degrees is warmer than -10 degrees.' Students who say '5 is more minus' or reverse the sentence can't yet interpret symbols back into context.

worked_solution.stem: On a horizontal number line, -8.25 is to the left of -6.34. Write an inequality to represent this statement.

steps.annotation: Position words pick the symbol. On a horizontal line, left means LESS -- always.

steps.math: -8.25 is left, so -8.25 is the lesser value.
steps.annotation: Sentence order and digit size don't matter. Only the position does.
Read it out loud: 'negative 8.25 is less than negative 6.34.' It matches the picture. (-6.34 > -8.25 says the same thing.)
